pedagogy.summary: At 9-11 gravity graduates from the intuitive 'things fall down' to a directional, universal FORCE: Earth pulls every object toward its CENTRE, so 'down' is not one fixed direction in the universe but 'toward the centre of the sphere' — which is why people all around the globe are all pulled 'down' toward the middle and nobody falls off. The same pulling force reaches out to hold the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun. The load-bearing shifts are (1) down = toward Earth's centre (a local, radial direction, not absolute), and (2) gravity is a long-reach attraction that also causes orbits — not something that switches off in space.
bestPractices: Confront the 'people fall off the bottom' puzzle head-on using a globe with figures stuck all around it: each person's feet point to the centre, so every one of them experiences 'down' as toward the middle — there is no universal up/down in space.

Build the argument from evidence (the NGSS framing): unsupported objects always fall toward Earth, and they fall toward the centre wherever you are on the planet — use this pattern to argue that Earth's gravity is directed inward/down.
Extend gravity's reach explicitly to orbits: the SAME pull that drops a ball also holds the Moon to Earth and planets to the Sun — gravity acts across empty space and does not need air or contact.

Directly reframe 'no gravity in space': astronauts float because they are in continual free-fall around Earth (Earth's gravity is still strong there), not because gravity has vanished — heading off the most common upper-primary error.
Keep it qualitative and directional at this age: gravity as a pulling force with a direction (toward the centre); reserve mass-vs-weight formalism and F–m–a for KS3.
keyRepresentations: Globe cross-section with stick-figures placed all around the rim, each with a 'down' arrow pointing to the centre
Dropped-object trails on a sphere: from any starting point the object heads toward Earth's centre
Newton's-cannonball style picture: turn the pull off and the Moon flies off in a straight line; turn it on and it curves into orbit
Sun-at-centre orbit diagram with gravity arrows from each planet pointing at the Sun
Free-fall astronaut image labelled 'still lots of gravity — falling around Earth', not 'zero gravity'
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 'down' is a single absolute direction in the universe, so people on the 'other side' of the globe should fall off — not grasping that down means toward Earth's centre for everyone.
Believing there is NO gravity in space, or that astronauts float because gravity has switched off — rather than being in continual free-fall/orbit with gravity still acting.
Thinking gravity needs air (an atmosphere) to work, so it couldn't act in the vacuum of space or on the airless Moon.
Assuming gravity only acts on things that are falling or unsupported, not realising it acts on everything all the time (including things at rest and objects in orbit).
Not connecting the everyday 'falling' force with the force that holds the Moon and planets in orbit — treating them as unrelated.
Believing heavier objects are pulled much harder and so always fall noticeably faster (the Aristotelian attractor), ignoring air resistance as the real everyday difference.

learn.summary: Help 9-11 year-olds reframe gravity from the intuitive 'things fall down' to a directional, universal pulling force: Earth attracts every object toward its CENTRE, so 'down' is not a single fixed cosmic direction but 'toward the centre of the sphere' for everyone — which is why people all around the globe stay firmly on the ground and nobody falls off. The same long-reach pull holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun, acting across empty space with no need for air or contact. Keep it qualitative and directional at this age; reserve mass-vs-weight formalism and F=ma for later. Core misconceptions to confront: 'down' as absolute (so the far side falls off), 'no gravity in space', gravity needing air, gravity only acting on falling/unsupported things, and heavier objects always falling noticeably faster.

activities.title: Everyone's 'down' points to the centre
feedback: If a learner says the far-side person is upside-down and could fall off: place figures all the way around the globe and draw each one's 'down' arrow — every arrow points to the centre, so nobody is upside-down relative to their own ground.

Prompt: 'If you dug a tunnel straight down from Britain and from Australia, would the tunnels point the same way in space, or nearly opposite ways?' (Nearly opposite ways — Australia isn't exactly opposite Britain — yet both are 'down' because both head to the centre.)
Reinforce: a child in Australia feels their feet firmly on the ground just as you do; there is no single fixed 'down' for the whole universe.
activities.rationale: The pivotal idea is a spatial RELATIONSHIP that convinces best when the learner places people anywhere on a sphere and sees every 'down' arrow re-aim at the centre, then sees (on screen) dropped objects all fall inward. This builds the argument from a repeatable pattern rather than assertion. A physical ball/globe and a cross-section diagram both carry the argument; an interactive version lets learners test 'what if I stand here?'

UK Year 5 Forces requires pupils to 'explain that unsupported objects fall towards the Earth because of the force of gravity acting between the Earth and the falling object'.
learnerActions: Using a globe (a physical ball, classroom globe, or an on-screen globe cross-section), place stick-figures all around it — top, sides, and the very bottom.
For each figure, draw or reveal a 'down' arrow from their feet and trace where it points; notice every arrow aims at the SAME place: the centre of the Earth.
Place one figure directly opposite yourself — standing 'upside-down' relative to you — and check that their 'down' still points to the middle.

On an on-screen model, use the drop-a-ball animation to release balls from several different positions and watch them all head inward toward the centre. On a physical globe, do this as a representational step instead — trace or draw each ball's path/arrow toward the model's centre — because real dropped balls fall toward the actual Earth, not toward a model globe's centre.
Answer aloud: 'If down means toward the centre, does anyone fall off? Why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: 'Down' is a local, radial direction — toward Earth's centre — not one fixed direction in the universe. Because every person's 'down' points to the centre, people all around the globe feel perfectly normal and nobody falls off, even though their 'down' points a different way in space from ours — and for someone directly opposite us, the opposite way.

activities.title: Same pull drops a ball and bends the Moon's path
feedback: If a learner says there's no gravity in space: gravity reaches out across space — it is exactly what holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun.
If a learner ties gravity to air: gravity acts in the airless vacuum of space too — the Moon has gravity and no air at all.
Prompt: 'What keeps the Moon circling instead of drifting off in a straight line?' (Earth's gravity continually bending its path.)
activities.rationale: Connecting the everyday falling force to orbits directly addresses the misconception that these are unrelated, and that gravity switches off in space. A predict-then-reveal 'gravity off → straight line' contrast makes the role of the force in curving the path concrete. An on/off toggle is one optional way to render this; a labelled before/after diagram also works. (The orbit extension is a pedagogy-derived link; it is kept qualitative and is not directly asserted by the cited sources.)
learnerActions: Study (or manipulate) a diagram of the Moon circling Earth with a gravity arrow pointing from the Moon toward Earth.

Predict: 'If the pull between Earth and Moon suddenly switched off, what path would the Moon take?' Then check in the simple Earth–Moon model (ignoring the Sun's pull) — with the pull off, the Moon moves off in a straight (tangent) line; with the pull on, that same pull curves its path into an orbit.
Repeat the idea with a Sun-at-centre diagram: each planet has a gravity arrow pointing at the Sun.
State in your own words how the force that drops a ball on Earth is the SAME force that keeps the Moon and planets in orbit.
Explain whether gravity needs air to work, using the airless Moon as evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Gravity is a long-reach attraction acting across empty space — no air or contact needed. The same pull that makes a ball fall is what bends the Moon's straight-line motion into an orbit around Earth, and the planets' paths around the Sun.

activities.title: Busting the 'zero gravity' myth
feedback: If a learner says gravity has switched off in space: the same pull holds the Moon in orbit; if gravity were gone, the ship and astronaut would fly off in a straight line, not circle Earth.
Reinforce that the astronaut and spacecraft fall together, so the astronaut appears to float relative to the craft.
Label the image honestly as 'still lots of gravity — falling around Earth', not 'zero gravity'.
activities.rationale: This heads off the most common upper-primary error directly and reuses the orbit reasoning from the previous activity, reinforcing that gravity acts continuously and across space. The free-fall explanation is drawn from standard physics-education guidance, though this source was not re-verified in this rewrite.
sourceClaims: Astronaut 'weightlessness' is continual free-fall (orbit) with Earth's gravity still acting, not the absence of gravity — a persistent upper-primary/secondary misconception.
learnerActions: Look at an image of an astronaut floating and discuss WHY they float.
Decide which explanation fits the evidence: (a) gravity has switched off, or (b) the astronaut and their ship are both falling around Earth together, with Earth's gravity still strongly acting.
Connect this to the orbit idea: being in orbit IS continual free-fall around Earth.
Answer: 'Is there gravity where astronauts are? How do you know?'
activities.intendedInsight: Astronauts float because they are in continual free-fall (orbit) around Earth, where Earth's gravity is still strong — not because gravity has vanished. 'Weightlessness' is free-fall, not absence of gravity.

activities.title: Check and reason: which way is 'down'?
feedback: Full understanding: explains gravity pulls toward Earth's centre so 'down' is centre-relative (opposite sides both feel normal), AND that the same pull keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits.

Partial: says gravity pulls 'down' and nobody falls off, but cannot clearly state 'down' means toward the centre, or doesn't connect gravity to orbits — revisit the arrow-drawing and orbit activities.
Gap: thinks the far side is upside-down and could fall off, or that there's no gravity in space — return to placing figures around the globe and drawing each 'down' arrow to the centre.
activities.rationale: A two-tier 'answer plus why' check discriminates between an absolute and a centre-relative notion of 'down', which recognition-only items can miss. This is a check on reasoning and should follow, not replace, the hands-on/interactive building activities.
sourceClaims: Grade-5 standard: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1]', with the clarification that '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS2-1].
learnerActions: Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'A child in Australia is on nearly the opposite side of the round Earth from a child in Britain. Are the people in Australia hanging upside down, in danger of falling off into space? What does "down" actually mean for them? Tell me WHY.'
Decide: is there one single 'down' for the whole universe, or does 'down' depend on where you're standing?
Match each cause to its effect: Earth's pull → a ball falls toward the centre; Earth's pull → the Moon orbits; the Sun's pull → planets orbit.
Judge true or false and justify: 'There is no gravity in space.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain WHY no one falls off — because 'down' is centre-relative, not absolute — is the crux. A learner who still holds an absolute 'down' thinks the far side hangs upside-down; a learner who understands the concept says everyone's feet point 'down' toward the centre and no one falls.

constraints: Keep gravity qualitative and directional at ages 9-11: a pulling force with a direction (toward the centre). Do not introduce mass-vs-weight formalism or F=ma — reserve for later stages.

A multiple-choice/true-false check (e.g. 'which way is down for a figure on the far side?', 'no gravity in space?') can confirm the argument and surface misconceptions, but recognition-only responses do not elicit the learner's own spatial reasoning or constructed 'why'; pair any such check with the arrow-drawing and explain-why tasks.

A labelled diagram or tap-to-reveal image can show the arrangement ('their down points to the centre too'; 'Moon held by Earth's gravity') but cannot let the learner test 'what if I stand here?' or 'what if gravity switched off?'; it is a strong low-cost scaffold, while a manipulable model supports learner-driven testing of those what-ifs.

A physical ball/globe with stuck-on figures and a flat cross-section diagram serve different purposes: the physical object gives authentic 3D spatial experience, the clean cross-section makes the radial 'down' arrows easy to read. Neither is universally required; use whichever makes the centre-directed pattern clearest. Note that real dropped balls fall toward the actual Earth, so the 'all fall to the centre' pattern on a physical model must be shown by drawn/traced arrows or an on-screen animation, not by literally dropping balls.

Any on/off toggle, draggable figures, live 'down' arrows, or dropped-ball animations are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms — the same insight can be reached with a physical globe, drawn arrows, and predict-then-check discussion.

Address the Aristotelian 'heavier always falls noticeably faster' idea when it arises: in everyday life air resistance, not weight, usually explains the difference; avoid implying heavier objects are 'pulled much harder so always fall faster'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any activity was tested.

Of the three sources, only the NGSS 5-PS2-1 claim is marked verified in the source row; the UK National Curriculum Year 5 claim and the astronaut free-fall/IOP Spark misconception claim are marked unverified. Treat their wording as legacy, not independently confirmed here.

The orbit extension in activity 2 (same pull bends the Moon's path; holds planets to the Sun) is a pedagogy-derived link, not directly asserted by any of the three cited source claims; its sourceClaims is therefore [] and the content is kept qualitative.

The legacy 'conversation is poor / dialogue cannot render the conviction' and 'coded 2D model does exactly this' framings were catalog fit rankings, not established efficacy claims; softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements and not asserted as universal laws.

Minor physics care for this age: the Moon's 'straight line if gravity off' is the tangent to its orbit (Newton's cannonball reasoning); keep it qualitative. 'Free-fall' means the spacecraft and astronaut accelerate toward Earth together, so the astronaut floats relative to the craft — state this carefully to avoid implying no force acts.

Activity 1's dropped-ball step was re-scoped: a literal drop on a physical globe falls toward the real Earth, not the model's centre, so that observation is valid only on screen or as a drawn/traced representation on a physical model.

probeDeeper: If you dug a tunnel straight down from Britain and from Australia, would the two tunnels point the same way in space, or opposite ways?
What keeps the Moon circling the Earth instead of drifting off in a straight line?
Is there gravity on the Moon, where there's no air?
Is there one single 'down' for the whole universe, or does 'down' depend on where you're standing?
assess.correctAnswer: No — nobody falls off, because gravity pulls everything toward the CENTRE of the Earth, and 'down' means 'toward Earth's centre' wherever you stand. For the child in Australia, 'down' points to the centre just as it does in Britain, so their feet are firmly on the ground and everything feels perfectly normal — even though their 'down' points the opposite way in space to ours. There is no single fixed 'down' in the universe; each person's down points to Earth's centre. (That same pull, reaching across space, is what keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and the planets orbiting the Sun.)

errorPatterns.pattern: people on the opposite side of the Earth are upside down and could fall off ('down' is one fixed direction in space)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place little figures all the way around a globe and draw each one's 'down' arrow — every arrow points to the centre; nobody is upside-down relative to the ground.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — people in Australia are upside down and would fall off if gravity weren't strong enough to hold them on.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child worries the far side hangs upside-down or falls off, treating 'down' as an absolute cosmic direction

errorPatterns.pattern: there is no gravity in space ('once you leave Earth, nothing pulls')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity reaches out across space — it is exactly what holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's no gravity in space, so nothing is pulled once you leave Earth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child denies gravity acts beyond Earth's surface

errorPatterns.pattern: gravity only works because of air / needs an atmosphere
errorPatterns.nextMove: Gravity acts in the airless vacuum of space too — the Moon has gravity and no air at all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child ties gravity to the presence of air

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the far side of the Earth is upside-down and could fall off, or that there's no gravity in space — treats 'down' as absolute.
responseLevels.full: Explains gravity pulls toward Earth's centre so 'down' is centre-relative (opposite sides both feel normal), and that the same pull keeps the Moon and planets in their orbits.
responseLevels.partial: Says gravity pulls 'down' and nobody falls off, but cannot clearly state that 'down' means toward the centre, or doesn't connect gravity to orbits.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child in Australia is on the exact opposite side of the round Earth from a child in Britain. Are the people in Australia hanging upside down, in danger of falling off into space? What does 'down' actually mean for them? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding an absolute 'down' (one fixed downward direction in space) believes the far side of the Earth hangs upside-down and could fall off. A child who understands gravity points toward the centre says everyone's feet are 'down' toward the centre and no one falls. The 'why' tier reveals whether 'down' is centre-relative or absolute — the crux of the concept.
